lives in the Google Doc, the same split as study_sources.json and the
Every topic carries a `project`, because the doc's own best section is
'BLOG IDEAS (with enforced projects)' and because docs/writing-standard.md
refuses generated prose. A topic without a project is a title you will
never have anything true to say under. The project is what produces the
evidence that content/pipeline.py then turns into the three levels.
`query` is the search it targets — the thing that makes this SEO rather
than vibes. Pick topics where you can out-specific the first page, not
out-rank it: 'aws multi-az vs read replica' has a thousand summaries and
Add topics by editing this file. `python3 content/topics.py --publish`
appends the next version to the doc; nothing is ever overwritten.
`tab` is the Google Doc tab a section is published into. The doc is eight
tabs, not eight headings — documents.get returns only the FIRST tab unless
you ask for includeTabsContent, which is how a whole bank once landed at

sections.title: AWS Solutions Architecture
sections.why: You are sitting SAA-C03 and you have no AWS writing. Publishing as you study is the cheapest portfolio there is: the work is already happening, and 'I measured this' outranks 'here is what AWS docs say' on every one of these queries.

topics.title: I rebuilt a Cloudflare Workers app on AWS Lambda — what each costs and where each breaks
topics.query: cloudflare workers vs aws lambda cost comparison
topics.project: Port one slice of Monster Agent: Workers to Lambda, cron triggers to EventBridge, Durable Object alarms to EventBridge Scheduler, Neon to RDS. Price both in the AWS Pricing Calculator and against your real Cloudflare bill.
topics.angle: Almost nobody has run the same non-trivial workload on both. This is the piece only you can write, it is SAA revision, and it is the interview answer for 'tell me about an architecture trade-off you made'.

topics.title: A 15-minute RTO costs this much: pricing the four AWS disaster recovery strategies
topics.query: aws disaster recovery cost comparison rto rpo
topics.project: Take one workload. Price backup/restore, pilot light, warm standby and multi-site in the Pricing Calculator. Publish the table and the RTO each actually buys.
topics.angle: The four strategies are described everywhere and costed nowhere. A real table is a permanent reference and a direct SAA domain.

topics.title: Multi-AZ is not a read replica: measuring RDS failover instead of describing it
topics.query: rds multi-az vs read replica difference
topics.project: Deploy both. Force a failover, time it with a client writing continuously. Record connection errors and seconds lost.
topics.angle: The single most confused distinction in the exam, and every article explains it without a number.

topics.title: Security groups vs NACLs, proven with packets rather than prose
topics.query: security group vs nacl stateful stateless
topics.project: Build a two-subnet VPC and break traffic four ways: SG ingress, SG egress, NACL ingress, NACL egress. Screenshot the flow logs for each.
topics.angle: Stateful vs stateless is a sentence everyone repeats. Showing the return traffic dropping is the thing that makes it stick.

topics.title: The VPC diagram that finally made it click — built in Terraform, not drawn
topics.query: aws vpc public private subnet nat gateway tutorial
topics.project: Two AZs, public and private subnets, IGW, NAT. Prove a private instance reaches the internet and nothing reaches it. Commit the Terraform.
topics.angle: The hardest SAA domain and the highest-volume query here. Yours ranks if the repo is runnable.

topics.title: Egress is the bill nobody models
topics.query: aws data transfer cost between availability zones
topics.project: Move a fixed payload cross-AZ, cross-region and out to the internet. Put the three costs side by side per GB.
topics.angle: Data transfer is where real AWS bills go wrong and where the cost-optimised domain hides. Nobody writes it with numbers.

topics.title: S3 lifecycle transitions: where the money actually goes, including retrieval
topics.query: s3 storage class lifecycle cost glacier retrieval
topics.project: Lifecycle a bucket Standard to IA to Glacier. Chart cost per GB-month, and then the retrieval cost and time nobody includes.
topics.angle: Every comparison stops at storage price. The retrieval cost is the part that bites.

topics.title: Running a Well-Architected review on your own side project
topics.query: aws well architected framework review example
topics.project: Run the real review against Monster Agent. Publish the findings, including the ones that embarrass you.
topics.angle: Reviews are published as checklists and never as results. A real one with real findings is both rare and exactly what an architect interview probes.

sections.title: System Design & Interview Prep (beginner to advanced)
sections.why: This section of the doc was an empty heading. These are the highest-intent queries you can target — people searching them are preparing for the same interviews you are — and every one doubles as your own revision.

topics.title: Turning an awesome-list into a study plan: how to actually read a system design repo
topics.query: how to study system design github repo
topics.project: Take liquidslr/system-design-notes and the primer. Produce a 6-week ordered plan with one narration per topic, and publish the plan itself.
topics.angle: Thousands star these repos and bounce off them. The plan is the product.

topics.title: The back-of-envelope numbers every interview assumes you already know
topics.query: latency numbers every programmer should know 2026
topics.project: Build the cheat sheet, then verify at least three numbers yourself on your own hardware and say where they differ.
topics.angle: The canonical list is fifteen years old. Re-measuring even three entries is a legitimate, citable update.

topics.title: Designing a rate limiter: token bucket vs sliding window, implemented and benchmarked
topics.query: token bucket vs sliding window rate limiter
topics.project: Implement both. Benchmark burst behaviour and memory. Show where each lets through traffic the other blocks.
topics.angle: The most common design question after the URL shortener, and almost always answered from memory rather than from code.

topics.title: Idempotency keys: the detail that separates a junior answer from a senior one
topics.query: idempotency key api design retry
topics.project: Build a payment endpoint that survives duplicate submits, client retries and a crash between write and response. Prove each case with a test.
topics.angle: You have already lived this — your webhook ingress and the nag engine both needed it. Write from the scar.

topics.title: Caching strategies, measured: write-through, write-back, write-around
topics.query: write through vs write back vs write around cache
topics.project: Three implementations over the same workload. Publish hit rates, staleness windows and what each loses on a crash.
topics.angle: Universally described as a diagram, never as a measurement.

topics.title: Why 'design a URL shortener' is a trick question
topics.query: url shortener system design interview
topics.project: Build it, then deliberately break it at the points interviewers probe: key collisions, hot keys, analytics writes drowning reads.
topics.angle: Enormous search volume and uniformly shallow results. The angle — what is actually being tested — is the differentiator.

topics.title: Consistent hashing, implemented and then rebalanced under load
topics.query: consistent hashing implementation virtual nodes
topics.project: Implement a ring with virtual nodes. Add and remove a node under live traffic and chart how many keys move.
topics.angle: Explained constantly, demonstrated rarely. The rebalance chart is the asset.

topics.title: The outbox pattern: exactly-once that survives a crash between the write and the publish
topics.query: transactional outbox pattern implementation
topics.project: Build a service that writes a row and publishes an event atomically. Kill it mid-flight and show no event lost and none duplicated.
topics.angle: The crash test is the whole article, and it is the part nobody shows.

topics.title: Reading someone else's architecture docs and finding the decision they did not write down
topics.query: how to read architecture decision records adr
topics.project: Take two open-source ADR sets. Find a decision implied by the code but absent from the record, and write the missing ADR.
topics.angle: You already keep architecture docs and agent.md. This demonstrates the skill interviews actually test — reconstructing intent from a system.

sections.title: AI Engineering
sections.why: Another empty heading, and the section with the most direct line to the Flow fellowship: every week of that programme produces a lab, and a lab plus a result is an article you already paid for.

topics.title: Tool calling breaks on malformed output — what a schema validator actually has to handle
topics.query: llm tool calling schema validation malformed json
topics.project: Build a two-tool pipeline with strict validation. Log every malformed response over a hundred runs and classify the failure modes.
topics.angle: This is fellowship week 6's lab. The taxonomy of failures is the contribution — everyone writes the happy path.

topics.title: An MCP server for your own tools, and what exposing them costs you
topics.query: model context protocol mcp server tutorial
topics.project: Re-expose the same two tools behind MCP. Compare integration effort, latency and failure surface against direct calling.
topics.angle: You run MCP servers in production already. The cost side is unwritten.

topics.title: The harness is the product: evaluating an agent you built
topics.query: llm agent evaluation harness benchmark
topics.project: Run your auditor against targets you solved by hand. Record found, missed and wrongly discarded. That table is the eval harness.
topics.angle: Agent demos are everywhere; agent evaluations are not. This is the single most credible thing you can publish in AI right now.

topics.title: RAG over your own documents, and the retrieval failures nobody screenshots
topics.query: rag retrieval failure modes chunking
topics.project: Build RAG over your own notes. Collect twenty queries it answers wrongly and classify why — chunking, embedding, or reranking.
topics.angle: Fellowship week 7. The failure gallery is the piece.

topics.title: What finetuning actually bought me, measured against a better prompt
topics.query: finetuning vs prompt engineering when worth it
topics.project: Take one task. Baseline with prompting, then finetune. Publish cost, latency and quality side by side, including the case where prompting won.
topics.angle: The honest negative result is rarer and more linkable than another finetuning tutorial.

sections.title: Web3 Security x AI (your differentiator)
sections.why: The doc is already deep on Web3 security and separately on AI. The intersection is where you have something almost nobody else has — a working auditing agent and the hand-solved findings to judge it against.

topics.title: I pointed an AI auditor at bugs I had already solved by hand. Here is what it missed.
topics.query: ai smart contract audit tool accuracy
topics.project: Run the auditor against five hand-solved targets. Publish found, missed, and wrongly discarded, with the PoC prompt that failed in each case.
topics.angle: Every AI audit tool publishes what it found. None publish what they missed. Being the one who does is the whole position.

topics.title: Turning a Solodit finding into an executable invariant
topics.query: smart contract invariant testing foundry
topics.project: Take ten findings. Restate each as an assertion a fuzzer can break, not a topic. Commit them to the knowledge YAML and show two that caught a regression.
topics.angle: 'Accounting should be correct' is not an invariant. 'totalBorrows + cash == totalSupplied - reserves' is. Showing the conversion is teachable and rare.

topics.title: The discard pile is the product: tuning an AI auditor's false-positive gate
topics.query: ai code audit false positive filtering
topics.project: Open a run's discard pile. For each, decide whether it was correctly discarded or the PoC prompt failed. Make one tuning change justified by a specific discard.
topics.angle: Precision work on agent output, with a real artifact — the commit. This is the Phase 6 eval work you already have scheduled.

topics.title: Reading a bridge exploit as an architect rather than an auditor
topics.query: cross chain bridge exploit post mortem analysis
topics.project: Take one bridge post-mortem. Rewrite it as an architecture decision record: what was traded away, when, and whether the trade was defensible at the time.
topics.angle: Bridges your two tracks together and is unusually strong in an interview, because it shows you reason about systems and not just bugs.
